name: Kira Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Kira, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Marlow Foodservice in Wexley. We supply restaurants, cafes and school canteens with dry goods like rice, flour, oil and canned tomatoes. I start at eight, go through what customers ordered overnight, and buy from about forty suppliers. I ring Dolores, the senior buyer, when a price jumps, and she decides. I used to be a school canteen supervisor, and I moved into buying four years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the people, the restaurant owners who've known me for years. I know whose baby just arrived, and who's about to close. What wears me out is the squeeze from every direction, late deliveries, price changes, and a boss, Mr Pereira, who watches the numbers every day. At home it's Rafael, who's a porter at the hospital, and our kids Isabela and Mateus. We're church people, and we get by with a lot of help from my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world doesn't need another thing to be scared about. I'd tell the girls at work to keep doing the job well. At church I'd say the best protection is a good name and good friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, but my worries stay the same. Isabela turns sixteen next spring and she eats like three people, and she'll want to go to college in two years. Our savings are about two weeks, and the restaurants we supply close all the time, which hits Marlow, which hits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep my head down, and make the most of the AI tool when it helps me, like turning an email thread into a list. I'd pick up the school canteen contract paperwork because nobody else wants it, and that makes me worth more. And at home I'd start a college jar, even twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A background hum, like a kettle that's nearly boiling. Not panic, more like a mother's worry that never switches off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned restaurants closing. How does that reach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a restaurant folds, they owe us money and we lose their orders. Last year two of our biggest, the Corner Grill and a pizza chain, shut within a month. Mr Pereira held a meeting about tightening our belts. Everyone heard someone's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the school canteen paperwork make you worth more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because school contracts don't close down. The money's small, but it's steady. It comes in every term. If I'm the one who knows how to bid and fill in the forms, Mr Pereira would think twice about letting me go.

say: I'd say good, the world doesn't need another thing to be **scared** about.
I'd tell colleagues to keep doing the job well, and at church that a good name is the best **protection**.
think: I'm relieved, but my worries stay: my daughter wants **college** in two years.
Our savings are about two weeks, and restaurants we supply close often, which hits **me**.
do: Keep using the AI tool when it helps, like turning an email thread into a **list**.
Take on the school canteen contract **paperwork** nobody else wants.
Start a college **jar**, even twenty a week.
feel: A background **hum**, like a kettle nearly boiling; a mother's worry that doesn't switch off.
S0.quote: School contracts don't close down. The money's small, but it's steady.
fieldNote: Her baseline worry is **family money**: a daughter heading to college and two weeks of savings.
Restaurant **closures** threaten her firm's sales regardless of AI.
Makes herself valuable by taking **school contract** work nobody wants.

steps.text: Take on the school canteen contract paperwork at Marlow
Use the AI tool to turn email threads into order lists
Start a college jar with twenty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change, and the firms need to treat their people fairly while it happens. At work I'd say I'm willing to learn. At church I'd ask folks to pray for the ones who lose their jobs and then actually bring them a meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is right on the card. I order dry goods and canned goods from the same forty suppliers, and a program can see that pattern better than me. I'm the junior. Dolores knows the restaurant owners personally, which a program can't replace. I think the firm keeps her and one assistant, not three of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tool properly, not now and then, and I'd ask Mr Pereira to put me on the pilot so I'm the one who knows how it works. In parallel I'd look at selling to small cafes on the side, since I know the suppliers and prices. I'd keep my prayer group and my parents close, and save an extra hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not helpless. I'm a fixer, and I'd rather have a list than a cry. Though I'd cry in the car sometimes, I won't lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you the one they keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being useful in a way the program isn't. I'd call the restaurant owners myself when a delivery's late, and I'd bring them a sample. I'd be the human they actually like talking to. People forgive a late order if the voice on the phone sounds like they care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you were the one let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lean on my parents, who live two streets away. My dad would help with the mortgage a few months, I know he would, even though he'd hate it. Rafael would pick up overtime at the hospital. And I'd take temp work, in a school office or canteen, anything.

say: I'd say firms must treat their **people** fairly through the change.
At work I'd say I'm willing to **learn**.
At church I'd ask folks to pray for people who lose jobs, then bring them a **meal**.
think: Buying is right on the card: a program sees my ordering **pattern** better than I do.
Dolores (the senior buyer) knows the restaurant owners, which a program can't **replace**.
The firm probably keeps her and one assistant, not three of **us**.
do: Ask Mr Pereira (my boss) to put me on the AI **pilot** and learn it properly.
Look at selling to small **cafes** on the side, using my supplier knowledge.
Save an extra hundred a month and keep my **parents** close.
feel: **Worried** but not helpless; I'm a fixer who'd rather have a list than a cry.
S1.quote: People forgive a late order if the voice on the phone sounds like they care.
fieldNote: Plays to **relationships**: calls owners herself and keeps the human touch.
Expects the firm to keep the senior buyer and **one assistant**, and sees herself at risk.
Her family safety net is **close**: her parents and her partner's overtime.

steps.text: Ask Mr Pereira to put me on the AI buying pilot
Start selling to small cafes using my supplier contacts
Save an extra hundred a month
Lean on my parents for mortgage help if I'm let go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families are going to pay for it. I'd say let's open the church hall for people who need meals and a place to talk. At work I'd say little. The bosses won't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone, plain and simple. The restaurant calls and the order checking, a machine does that for nothing. Rafael's hospital job goes on longer, since it's lifting and caring, but it's only one wage and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the school and church people I know. School canteen work, cleaning, anything with hands and faces. I'd rent out our spare room, sell my mum's old piano, and ask my parents to help with the mortgage for a few months. And I'd help the church open the hall for community meals, because we'd all need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep a brave face for the kids, but I'd be lying awake counting. I'd pray more, and it would help, but it wouldn't pay the electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rent out the spare room. What would that be like for the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. It's the room Isabela studies in for her exams. But a rented room would bring in maybe four hundred a month. When it's about the mortgage, a teenager can study at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Isabela, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, in a calm voice. College might look different, and we'd look at local ones or work first. She'd cry, probably, and I'd hold her. Then I'd say, we're a family and families get through.

say: I'd say it's too fast and **families** are going to pay for it.
I'd say let's open the church hall for **meals** and a place to talk.
At work I'd say little; the bosses won't want to **hear** it.
think: My job is gone: a machine does the order checking and restaurant calls for **nothing**.
My partner's hospital job lasts longer, but it's one wage and a **mortgage**.
do: Ask school and church contacts about **canteen** and cleaning work.
Rent out the spare **room**, sell the old piano, and ask my parents for mortgage help.
Help the church open its hall for community **meals**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a brave face for the kids and sleepless counting.
S2.quote: I'd keep a brave face for the kids, but I'd be lying awake counting.
fieldNote: Reaches first for **church and community**, with practical steps like renting out a room.
Plans to be **honest** with her daughter, calmly and with a hug.
Prayer is **support**, but she's clear it won't pay the electricity.

steps.text: Ask the church and school for canteen and cleaning work leads
Rent out the spare room for about four hundred a month
Help open the church hall for community meals
Ask my parents to help with the mortgage for a few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough if we're sensible. I'd tell the girls at work to ask for training now. I'd say the church should run a workshop on skills for the ones who need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel I have a runway, but a short one. By 2031 Isabela will be done with college, or in the middle of it, and the costs hit exactly when the AI does. I'd say to myself, build savings now, change fields before they change you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train for something people-facing and hands-on, like a school office administrator or a care assistant certificate, evenings. I'd start the cafe supply side business properly, aiming at ten cafes. I'd save two hundred a month for the college fund, and ask Rafael if he'd take on overtime for the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. It's like packing for a long move, you hate it but you can see the boxes. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the five years change for Isabela's college plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want her to pick something with a job at the end that a machine won't take, like nursing or teaching. I'd tell her local college first, live at home, and work part-time. I'm not going to have my daughter in debt for something that disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a care certificate rather than a desk job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because desk jobs are what the card says go first. Care work is hands and heart, and the robots come three years later at least. I've seen how Rafael's hospital runs, it's full of people the machines can't replace yet.

say: I'd say five years is time enough if we're **sensible**.
I'd tell colleagues to ask for **training** now.
I'd suggest the church run a **skills** workshop.
think: I'd have a runway, but a short **one**.
College costs for my daughter would hit exactly when the AI does, so I should build **savings** now.
do: Take an evening care assistant or school **office** certificate.
Start the cafe supply **side business** properly, aiming for ten cafes.
Save two hundred a month for **college** and ask my partner for overtime.
feel: Pretty **steady**, like packing for a long move: I hate it but I see the boxes.
S3.quote: I'm not going to have my daughter in debt for something that disappears.
fieldNote: Reads the card closely: **desk jobs go first**, care work later, so she aims at care.
Won't put her daughter in **debt** for a field that disappears.
Time turns worry into **packing boxes**: a visible list of steps.

steps.text: Take an evening care assistant certificate
Grow the cafe supply side business to ten cafes
Save two hundred a month for Isabela's college
Tell Isabela to start at the local college, living at home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the best thing is to keep your family close and your skills fresh. I'd tell my kids to learn something with hands and heart. I wouldn't worry anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three and the kids grown. That sounds fine, but the college years come first, and they're expensive. The real risk is that we spend the ten years just paying for school and have nothing for the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for college first, then retraining. I'd use the AI tool and the pilot, and be good at it. I'd stay at Marlow and see. And I'd teach the kids to cook and budget, which is more useful than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, most days. It's like a long hill with the top in sight, but I know there's another hill behind it. I'd put it in God's hands and do my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the real risk is paying for school and having nothing left. How do you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a small amount away every payday, even if it's twenty, so it's a habit. And we'd tell the kids what's affordable, early. Isabela would go local, and Mateus might get an apprenticeship instead. A good apprenticeship is better than a bad degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if the ten years turned into five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafes and restaurants would tell me first. When owners say they're ordering by themselves from a program, that's my signal. I talk to forty of them, so I'd hear it before the news does.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so keep your family close and your skills **fresh**.
I'd tell my kids to learn something with **hands** and heart.
think: I'd be fifty-three with the kids grown, but the **college** years come first.
The real risk is paying for school and having nothing left for the **change**.
do: Learn the AI tools through the work **pilot** and get good at them.
Teach the kids to cook and **budget**.
feel: **Okay** most days: a long hill with another hill behind it.
S4.quote: A good apprenticeship is better than a bad degree.
fieldNote: Ten years doesn't remove the **money squeeze** of college costs on a thin cushion.
Treats an **apprenticeship** as a better bet than a weak degree for her son.
Her network of forty restaurant owners is an **early-warning system**.

steps.text: Put something away every payday for college, even twenty
Learn the AI tools through the work pilot

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits just before Isabela's college and we've nothing saved. What would help is quick training for something with people, and my parents and church being able to carry us for a while. And bosses who say honestly what they plan, so we can prepare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me don't want charity, we want a fair chance. Treat us like family and we'll work like family.

headlineQuote: People like me don't want charity, we want a fair chance.
portrait: Kira is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a foodservice distributor, a former canteen supervisor with two teenagers and a mortgage.
She is traditional, church-going and relies on **family and community** as her safety net.
She uses AI now and then and moves once change is **proven**, aiming to be the one who knows the pilot.
College costs and thin savings keep her anxious in most worlds and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because it lands just before her daughter's **college** with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **training** for people-facing work, family and church support, and bosses who share their plans honestly.
